# On the Quiet Art of Noticing

There's something that happens in the last hour of daylight that I've never been able to properly explain. The shadows grow long and golden, and everything — *everything* — looks slightly more important than it did ten minutes ago. A crack in the sidewalk becomes a river canyon. A leaf spinning in the gutter becomes the slow orbit of something around something else entirely.

I think most people rush past this hour. They're driving home, or cooking dinner, or scrolling through the infinite feed of other people's attention. And I get it. I do that too. But occasionally — maybe when I'm walking without a destination, or sitting on a porch that doesn't belong to me — I catch the world mid-yawn, stretching out into its evening form, and it strikes me how much of life is just **waiting to be seen**.

We treat noticing as passive. As though the world does all the work. But it isn't passive. It requires a kind of deliberate softness — a willingness to let your guard down enough that the ordinary can register as strange again. Children are natural noticers. They'll stop on the sidewalk for a puddle and fill it with a universe. Somewhere along the way we learn to keep walking.

Maybe that's what art really is: the refusal to keep walking.

It's a coat draped over the shoulders of the mundane, saying *wait — look — this particular corner of existence, this exact quality of light, this specific arrangement of things that will never happen again — this deserves a second.*

I don't think you need to be talented to do this. You just need to occasionally stand still long enough for the world to reveal that it was always doing something remarkable and simply didn't have anyone watching.

And here's the part I find genuinely encouraging: **it doesn't stop**. The light will do something astonishingly different tomorrow evening. A cloud will pass over something in a way it never has before. A stranger will say something in a particular tone that catches somewhere in your chest. The world is endlessly inventive, endlessly generous, and it doesn't require an audience — but it seems to prefer one.

So maybe the best thing any of us can do, on any given day, is simply pay attention. Not to everything. Not all the time. Just *here* and *now* and whatever is happening to be here and now, which — if we're honest — is always something.
